questions.question: Describe the map of colonial Africa in 1914, naming the colonising countries and examples of their territories.
questions.expected_answer: Britain held Egypt and Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, Uganda, British East Africa (Kenya), Nyasaland, Northern and Southern Rhodesia, Bechuanaland, Basutoland, Swaziland, the Union of South Africa as a dominion, British Somaliland, and in West Africa Nigeria, the Gold Coast, Sierra Leone and the Gambia; German East Africa blocked Rhodes's Cape-to-Cairo dream. France held the largest area: French West Africa, French Equatorial Africa, Algeria, Tunisia, most of Morocco from 1912, Madagascar and French Somaliland. Germany held Togoland, Kamerun, German South West Africa and German East Africa, lost after the First World War. Belgium held the Belgian Congo from 1908. Portugal held Angola, Mozambique, Portuguese Guinea and islands. Italy held Eritrea, Italian Somaliland and Libya, seized in 1911 to 1912. Spain held Spanish Morocco, Rio de Oro and Spanish Guinea. Only Ethiopia, which defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896, and Liberia were independent.

questions.question: Explain the economic causes of the colonisation of Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Industrialisation created a demand for raw materials Europe could not supply cheaply, such as palm oil for soap, candles and lubrication, rubber for tyres, hoses and insulation, cotton, cocoa, coffee, groundnuts, timber and minerals like gold, diamonds and copper. Factories produced more than home markets could buy, so colonies were sought as markets that could be forced to buy goods from the colonising country. European investors sought profitable investments in mines, plantations, railways and trade, and chartered companies such as the Royal Niger Company, the Imperial British East Africa Company and the British South Africa Company governed and traded in territories. The Long Depression from 1873 encouraged protectionism, and colonies were seen as secure sources and markets. Hobson in 1902 and Lenin in 1917 argued imperialism was driven by capitalist investment, while other historians note that many colonies were not profitable at first and stress political causes; most combine explanations.

questions.question: Explain the political, strategic and social causes of colonisation and the role of technology.
questions.expected_answer: Nationalism made empire a symbol of power and prestige, helping France recover after defeat in 1870 to 1871 and showing that unified Germany and Italy were great powers. Rivalry meant powers rushed to claim land before rivals, explaining the speed of the scramble. Strategic interests included protecting the Suez Canal route to India, leading Britain to occupy Egypt in 1882 and later Sudan, and securing the Cape route, ports, coaling stations and bases. Missionaries sought to spread Christianity and often called for colonial protection, though some criticised abuses. The so-called civilising mission rested on racist beliefs of European superiority supported by pseudo-science such as social Darwinism, expressed in phrases like the white man's burden; these ideas are false and were used to justify conquest. Some saw colonies as places for settlement. Technology, including steamships, railways, the telegraph, quinine against malaria, breech-loading rifles and the Maxim gun of 1884, made colonisation possible, and the causes reinforced each other.
